name: Artificial hair integrations

lead: Artificial hair integrations blend human or synthetic hair into your own to add length, volume and coverage, and to camouflage hair loss from conditions such as alopecia. The fuller look is there as soon as they are applied.
Added hair is clipped, bonded, sewn, fused or pulled through a mesh base so it merges with existing hair. Attachment methods include tape-in, clip-in, micro rings, fusion, weaving and wigs.

paras: They are non-surgical and reversible, used for styling and for hair-loss coverage. Synthetic fibre such as Kanekalon costs much less than human hair but wears out faster under heat and friction. No clinical trials were found.
Prolonged tension, such as tight braiding, can cause traction alopecia, and adhesives are linked to skin reactions, dermatitis and headaches.

angle.text: Users with thinning hair or alopecia use weaves, hairpieces and integration systems to add length, volume and coverage right away. Added hair is attached to their own so thin areas are covered; traction and adhesive issues are documented separately.

lead: Artificial hair integrations are prosthetic hair products, such as extensions, weaves, hairpieces and mesh-based integration systems, that add length, volume or coverage to a person's own hair using human or synthetic fibre. They are used for styling and to camouflage hair loss from conditions such as alopecia [1][2].

Wikipedia lists attachment methods including tape-in, clip-in, micro rings, fusion, weaving and wigs, and notes that synthetic fibre such as Kanekalon costs much less than human hair but wears out faster under heat and friction [2]. Reported risks include traction alopecia from tight braiding and skin reactions to adhesives [1][2].
infobox: Human hair or synthetic fibre such as Kanekalon [2]
Clip, tape, bond, sew, thread, mesh [2]

paras: Human hair is sourced largely from Vietnam, India and China, with India, Singapore and Pakistan the largest exporters according to Wikipedia [2]. Synthetic options use fibres such as Kanekalon, and Futura is a more heat-tolerant polyester that cannot be coloured [2]. Integration systems pull natural hair through a perforated mesh base to blend with added strands [1].

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, dates artificial hairpieces to ancient Egypt around 3400 BC [1]. Wikipedia reports that wigs were fashionable in the late 17th century, that weaves appeared among celebrities in the 1950s and spread in the 1970s, and that Kanekalon was developed by Kaneka in the 1950s [2].

Wigs and extensions are worn by people with alopecia totalis and by people experiencing hair loss from treatments such as chemotherapy [2]. Grokipedia states dermatologists recommend them as non-invasive complements to minoxidil or surgery for some women with androgenetic alopecia [1].

Wikipedia reports hair loss along the front hairline or above the ears from prolonged wear, linked to traction alopecia that can become permanent with tight braiding, and glue linked to headaches, bald spots and dermatitis. It mentions patch testing [2].

timeline.event: Weaves appear among celebrities; Kanekalon developed [2]
